title: Introduction to Earth and Life Science
lesson:
Earth and Life Science is the study of Earth, its materials and systems, and the living organisms that exist on the planet. It combines concepts from Earth Science and Life Science to help students understand how Earth works, how it changes over time, and how living organisms depend on and interact with their surroundings.

Earth Science focuses on the physical aspects of Earth, including its structure, materials, atmosphere, water, landforms, and natural processes. It helps explain phenomena such as earthquakes, volcanic activity, weather, erosion, and the movement of Earth's different systems.

Life Science focuses on living organisms and their characteristics, structures, life processes, interactions, and diversity. It includes the study of plants, animals, microorganisms, and other forms of life, as well as how organisms grow, reproduce, adapt, and interact with one another.

Earth and Life Science are closely connected because living organisms are part of Earth's systems. Organisms depend on resources such as water, air, sunlight, and nutrients, while living organisms can also affect their environment.
discussion:
Earth is made up of interconnected systems that support life. These include the geosphere, which consists of the solid parts of Earth; the hydrosphere, which includes Earth's water; the atmosphere, which is the layer of gases surrounding Earth; and the biosphere, which includes areas where life exists.

Changes in one Earth system can affect other systems. For example, changes in rainfall can influence soil conditions and water availability, which can then affect plant growth and the organisms that depend on plants. Similarly, human activities can change environmental conditions and influence ecosystems.

Life Science helps us understand how organisms respond to these environmental conditions. Plants, animals, and microorganisms have different characteristics and adaptations that allow them to survive in particular environments. Studying these relationships helps explain the diversity of life found on Earth.

Understanding Earth and Life Science is also useful in studying environmental concerns. Topics such as climate, natural hazards, biodiversity, pollution, and the use of natural resources involve interactions between Earth's physical systems and living organisms.
example: Studying how plants depend on sunlight, water, soil, and air involves both Earth and Life Science. Life Science helps explain how the plant grows and performs its life processes, while Earth Science helps explain the environmental resources and conditions that support the plant.
keyTakeaway: Earth and Life Science helps students understand how Earth works and how living organisms depend on and interact with Earth's systems. By studying both the physical processes of Earth and the characteristics of living organisms, students can better understand the connections between the planet, its environment, and the diverse forms of life it supports.
keyConcepts: Earth and Life Science combines concepts from Earth Science and Life Science.
Earth Science focuses on Earth's materials, systems, structure, and physical processes.
Life Science focuses on living organisms, their characteristics, life processes, interactions, and diversity.
Earth's geosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere, and biosphere are interconnected.
Earth provides the conditions and resources necessary for life.
Living organisms depend on and interact with their environment.
Changes in one Earth system can affect other systems and living organisms.
Understanding Earth and Life Science helps explain environmental processes and concerns.

title: The Origin and Structure of the Earth
lesson:
Earth formed approximately 4.6 billion years ago from materials associated with the formation of the solar system. Over a very long period of time, these materials came together and gradually formed the planet. As Earth developed, heat and gravity caused its materials to separate according to their properties and densities, resulting in the formation of different internal layers.

The major internal layers of Earth are the crust, mantle, outer core, and inner core. The crust is the thin, solid outer layer where humans, plants, and many other organisms live. Beneath the crust is the mantle, a much thicker layer made mostly of hot, solid rock that can slowly deform and flow over long periods.

The outer core is located beneath the mantle and consists mainly of liquid iron and nickel. The inner core is the central part of Earth and is composed mainly of solid iron and nickel. The movement of material in the outer core contributes to Earth's magnetic field.

Earth can also be studied through several interconnected systems. These include the geosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere, and biosphere. These systems interact with one another and influence the conditions that make life possible.
discussion:
Earth's internal structure is important because the different layers have different compositions, temperatures, and physical properties. The crust is the outermost layer and varies in thickness depending on whether it forms part of the continents or the ocean floor. Beneath it, the mantle contains extremely hot material that can move slowly and contribute to processes such as plate movement.

The movement of Earth's tectonic plates is connected to processes occurring within the planet. Tectonic activity can result in earthquakes, volcanic activity, mountain building, and the formation of different landforms. These processes show that Earth is not a completely static planet but one that continues to change.

Earth can also be understood through its major systems. The geosphere includes rocks, soil, landforms, and Earth's solid interior. The hydrosphere includes oceans, rivers, lakes, groundwater, glaciers, and other forms of water. The atmosphere is the layer of gases surrounding Earth, while the biosphere includes living organisms and the areas where life exists.

These systems do not operate separately. For example, rainfall from the atmosphere can enter rivers and groundwater in the hydrosphere. Water can weather and erode rocks in the geosphere, while plants and other organisms in the biosphere depend on water, soil, air, and sunlight. These interactions demonstrate how Earth's systems are connected.
example: The ground where people live is part of the geosphere, while the water in rivers, lakes, and oceans belongs to the hydrosphere. When rain falls from the atmosphere and enters the soil, it connects the atmosphere, hydrosphere, and geosphere. Plants growing in the soil are part of the biosphere and depend on these systems for water and nutrients.
keyTakeaway: Earth has a complex internal structure made up of the crust, mantle, outer core, and inner core, as well as interconnected systems that include the geosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere, and biosphere. Understanding these structures and systems helps explain Earth's natural processes, changes, and ability to support different forms of life.
keyConcepts: Earth formed approximately 4.6 billion years ago from materials associated with the formation of the solar system.
Earth's materials gradually separated and formed different internal layers.
The crust is Earth's outer solid layer.
The mantle lies beneath the crust and is the thickest major internal layer.
The outer core is mainly liquid iron and nickel.
The inner core is mainly solid iron and nickel.
Earth's geosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere, and biosphere are interconnected.
Interactions among Earth's systems contribute to natural processes and support life.

title: Earth's Internal Structure and Plate Tectonics
lesson:
Earth's outer rigid layer, called the lithosphere, is divided into large pieces known as tectonic plates. These plates include parts of Earth's crust and the rigid uppermost portion of the mantle. They move slowly over a softer, more flexible layer of the upper mantle called the asthenosphere.

The movement and interaction of these tectonic plates are explained by the theory of plate tectonics. Although plates move very slowly, their movement over millions of years can produce significant changes to Earth's surface.

There are three major types of plate boundaries: divergent, convergent, and transform boundaries. At divergent boundaries, plates move away from one another. At convergent boundaries, plates move toward one another. At transform boundaries, plates slide horizontally past each other.

Plate movement contributes to many geological processes, including earthquakes, volcanic activity, mountain formation, and the creation or destruction of parts of Earth's crust.
discussion:
Tectonic plates move because of processes and forces associated with Earth's internal heat and the movement of material within the mantle. The movement is generally very slow, often only a few centimeters per year, but its effects can become significant over long periods.

At a divergent boundary, two plates move apart. As the plates separate, magma from beneath Earth's surface can rise and cool, forming new crust. Divergent boundaries commonly occur along mid-ocean ridges and can contribute to the formation of new oceanic crust.

At a convergent boundary, two plates move toward each other. Depending on the types of plates involved, one plate may be forced beneath another through a process called subduction. Subduction can produce deep ocean trenches, earthquakes, and volcanic activity. When two continental plates collide, their movement can contribute to the formation of large mountain ranges.

At a transform boundary, two plates slide horizontally past one another. Friction can cause stress to build up along the boundary. When the accumulated stress is released, it can produce an earthquake.

These different types of plate interactions demonstrate that Earth's surface is constantly changing. Geological features such as mountains, volcanoes, ocean trenches, and fault zones can be connected to the movement and interaction of tectonic plates.
example: When two tectonic plates move toward each other and one plate is forced beneath the other, the process is called subduction. Subduction can cause earthquakes and volcanic activity and can contribute to the formation of deep ocean trenches.
keyTakeaway: Plate tectonics explains how the slow movement and interaction of Earth's tectonic plates can produce major changes on the planet's surface. Through divergent, convergent, and transform boundaries, plate movement contributes to the formation of landforms and geological events such as earthquakes and volcanic activity.
keyConcepts: The lithosphere is Earth's rigid outer layer.
The lithosphere is divided into large tectonic plates.
Tectonic plates move slowly over the asthenosphere.
Plate tectonics explains the movement and interaction of Earth's tectonic plates.
Divergent boundaries occur when plates move apart.
Convergent boundaries occur when plates move toward one another.
Transform boundaries occur when plates slide past one another.
Subduction occurs when one tectonic plate moves beneath another.
Plate movement can contribute to earthquakes, volcanic activity, mountain formation, and other geological processes.

title: Minerals and Rocks
lesson:
A mineral is a naturally occurring, inorganic solid that has a definite chemical composition and an ordered internal structure. Minerals are the basic components of many rocks and can be identified through properties such as color, hardness, luster, streak, cleavage, and density.

A rock is a naturally occurring solid material made of one or more minerals or other mineral-like materials. Rocks are important components of Earth's crust and can form in different environments and through different geological processes.

Rocks are commonly classified into three major types: igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic. Igneous rocks form when molten material such as magma or lava cools and solidifies. Sedimentary rocks form from the accumulation, compaction, and cementation of sediments or through other sedimentary processes. Metamorphic rocks form when existing rocks are changed by heat, pressure, or chemically active fluids without completely melting.
discussion:
Minerals have a specific chemical composition and an organized arrangement of atoms. Different minerals have different physical and chemical properties, which allow geologists to identify and classify them. Common minerals include quartz, feldspar, mica, and calcite. Minerals can also be valuable resources used in construction, manufacturing, technology, and other human activities.

Igneous rocks form when molten rock material cools. When magma cools slowly beneath Earth's surface, it can form coarse-grained intrusive igneous rocks. When lava cools quickly at or near Earth's surface, it can form fine-grained or glassy extrusive igneous rocks.

Sedimentary rocks develop through processes involving sediments. Weathering can break existing rocks into smaller pieces, while erosion transports these materials to other locations. The sediments may eventually be deposited, compacted, and cemented together. Some sedimentary rocks can also form from the remains of organisms or from minerals that precipitate from water.

Metamorphic rocks form when existing rocks are exposed to conditions of increased heat, pressure, or chemically active fluids. The original rock does not completely melt. Instead, its minerals or texture may change, producing a new metamorphic rock. For example, limestone can change into marble, while shale can change into slate under appropriate metamorphic conditions.

These three rock types are connected through the rock cycle. A rock can be broken down into sediments, transformed by heat and pressure, or melted and later cooled into a new igneous rock. This means that Earth's rocks can change from one type to another over geological periods.
example: When lava cools and solidifies at Earth's surface, it can form an igneous rock such as basalt. If that rock is later exposed to weathering and erosion, its materials may become sediments that can eventually form a sedimentary rock. Under sufficient heat and pressure, the rock may also undergo metamorphism.
keyTakeaway: Minerals and rocks are important components of Earth's crust and form through different geological processes. The three major rock types—igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic—can undergo changes through the rock cycle, showing that Earth's materials are continuously transformed over time.
keyConcepts: Minerals are naturally occurring, inorganic solids with definite chemical compositions and ordered internal structures.
Minerals are important components of many rocks.
Rocks are naturally occurring solid materials made of minerals or other mineral-like materials.
Igneous rocks form from cooling magma or lava.
Sedimentary rocks form through processes involving sediments or other sedimentary materials.
Metamorphic rocks form when existing rocks are altered by heat, pressure, or chemically active fluids without completely melting.
The rock cycle describes how rocks can change from one type to another.
Minerals and rocks are important natural resources and components of Earth's crust.

title: Weathering, Erosion, and the Rock Cycle
lesson:
Weathering is the breakdown or alteration of rocks and minerals at or near Earth's surface. It can occur through physical processes that break rocks into smaller pieces or through chemical processes that change the minerals within rocks.

Physical weathering breaks rocks into smaller pieces without changing their chemical composition. Changes in temperature, the growth of plant roots, abrasion, and the action of ice can contribute to physical weathering.

Chemical weathering occurs when minerals in rocks are changed through chemical reactions. Water, oxygen, carbon dioxide, and acids produced naturally in the environment can contribute to these reactions.

Erosion is the movement of weathered rock and soil materials from one location to another. Water, wind, ice, and gravity are important agents of erosion. When transported materials eventually settle in a new location, the process is called deposition.

These processes are connected to the rock cycle, in which rocks continuously form and change through processes such as weathering, erosion, deposition, compaction, cementation, melting, cooling, heat, and pressure.
discussion:
Weathering is an important process in shaping Earth's surface. Physical weathering can cause large rocks to break into smaller fragments. For example, repeated heating and cooling can cause rocks to expand and contract, eventually contributing to cracks. Plant roots can also grow into small cracks and gradually widen them as the roots become larger.

Chemical weathering changes the minerals that make up rocks. For example, water and oxygen can react with certain minerals, causing them to break down or form new substances. Carbon dioxide dissolved in water can also contribute to chemical weathering of some types of rock.

Once rocks and minerals have been weathered, their materials can be transported through erosion. Flowing water can carry sediments along rivers, while wind can move loose particles across land. Glaciers can transport rocks and sediments as they move, and gravity can cause loose materials to move downhill.

When the energy of the transporting agent decreases, the sediments may settle. This process is called deposition. Over time, deposited sediments can accumulate in layers. Through compaction and cementation, these sediments may eventually become sedimentary rock.

Weathering, erosion, and deposition are therefore important parts of the rock cycle. Rocks can also undergo other processes. Heat and pressure can transform existing rocks into metamorphic rocks, while melting can produce magma. When magma or lava cools and solidifies, it can form igneous rocks.

The rock cycle shows that rocks are not permanent in their original form. Different geological processes can gradually change them from one type of rock into another over very long periods of time.
example: Rainwater can gradually break down exposed rock through physical and chemical weathering. Flowing water may then carry the resulting sediments to another location. When the water slows down, the sediments can settle through deposition and may eventually become part of a sedimentary rock.
keyTakeaway: Weathering, erosion, and deposition continuously change Earth's surface materials and contribute to the rock cycle. Through these and other geological processes, rocks can be broken down, transported, deposited, transformed, melted, or formed again over long periods of time.
keyConcepts: Weathering is the breakdown or alteration of rocks and minerals at or near Earth's surface.
Physical weathering breaks rocks into smaller pieces without changing their chemical composition.
Chemical weathering changes minerals through chemical reactions.
Erosion is the movement of weathered materials from one location to another.
Water, wind, ice, and gravity are important agents of erosion.
Deposition occurs when transported sediments settle in a new location.
Weathering, erosion, and deposition can contribute to the formation of sedimentary rocks.
The rock cycle describes the continuous formation and transformation of rocks.
Heat, pressure, melting, cooling, weathering, erosion, and deposition can all contribute to changes in Earth's rocks.

title: The Atmosphere and Earth's Systems
lesson:
The atmosphere is the layer of gases surrounding Earth. It contains gases such as nitrogen, oxygen, and smaller amounts of other gases that are important to Earth's environment and living organisms. The atmosphere helps regulate temperature, supports weather and climate processes, and provides gases needed by many forms of life.

The atmosphere interacts with the other major Earth systems: the geosphere, hydrosphere, and biosphere. These systems are not separate from one another. They continuously exchange materials and energy, creating connections that influence Earth's environment.

The hydrosphere includes all of Earth's water, such as oceans, rivers, lakes, groundwater, glaciers, and water vapor. The geosphere includes Earth's solid components, such as rocks, soil, landforms, and the solid parts of the planet. The biosphere includes living organisms and the areas of Earth where life exists.
discussion:
Earth's systems work together through different natural processes. The atmosphere interacts with the hydrosphere through processes such as evaporation, condensation, and precipitation. Water from oceans, lakes, rivers, and other bodies of water can evaporate into the atmosphere. As water vapor cools, it can condense and form clouds. Water may then return to Earth's surface as rain or other forms of precipitation.

The atmosphere also interacts with the geosphere. Wind and precipitation can contribute to the weathering and erosion of rocks and soil. At the same time, landforms and the Earth's surface can influence wind patterns, temperature, and the distribution of precipitation.

The biosphere is also closely connected to the atmosphere. Plants use carbon dioxide from the atmosphere during photosynthesis and release oxygen as part of the process. Animals and other organisms depend on atmospheric gases for their life processes. In turn, living organisms can influence Earth's systems through activities such as respiration, decomposition, and changes in vegetation.

The four systems can interact at the same time. For example, rainfall from the atmosphere can enter the hydrosphere, flow across the geosphere, and provide water needed by organisms in the biosphere. This demonstrates that a change in one system can affect conditions in the others.
example: Water evaporates from oceans and other bodies of water and enters the atmosphere as water vapor. The water vapor can condense into clouds and later return to Earth's surface through precipitation. The water may then flow through rivers and soil while being used by plants and animals. This demonstrates the interaction of the atmosphere, hydrosphere, geosphere, and biosphere.
keyTakeaway: Earth's atmosphere, hydrosphere, geosphere, and biosphere are interconnected systems that constantly interact with one another. Understanding these relationships helps explain how natural processes occur and how changes in one part of Earth can influence other parts of the environment.
keyConcepts: The atmosphere is the layer of gases surrounding Earth.
The hydrosphere includes Earth's water in its different forms and locations.
The geosphere includes Earth's solid components, such as rocks, soil, and landforms.
The biosphere includes living organisms and areas where life exists.
Earth's systems continuously exchange materials and energy.
The water cycle demonstrates interactions between the atmosphere and hydrosphere.
Weathering and erosion connect the atmosphere and hydrosphere with the geosphere.
Living organisms interact with and depend on the atmosphere, hydrosphere, and geosphere.
Changes in one Earth system can influence other systems.

title: Characteristics of Living Things
lesson:
Living organisms share several characteristics that distinguish them from nonliving matter. Although organisms vary greatly in size, structure, and complexity, they perform essential life processes that allow them to survive and continue their species.

One of the basic characteristics of life is that living organisms are made of one or more cells. Cells are the basic structural and functional units of life. Some organisms, such as many bacteria, consist of a single cell, while plants, animals, and other complex organisms are made up of many cells.

Living organisms also use energy to carry out life processes. The collection of chemical reactions that occur within an organism is called metabolism. Organisms obtain and use energy for activities such as growth, movement, repair, reproduction, and maintaining their internal conditions.

Living things grow and develop, reproduce, respond to stimuli, and maintain relatively stable internal conditions. The maintenance of stable internal conditions is known as homeostasis. Organisms also interact with their environments and may change or adapt over generations through evolutionary processes.
discussion:
Cells allow living organisms to perform the processes necessary for life. In multicellular organisms, different cells may have specialized structures and functions. These cells work together to form tissues, organs, and organ systems that allow the organism to function properly.

Living organisms need energy to perform their life processes. Plants can capture light energy through photosynthesis, while animals obtain energy by consuming food. At the cellular level, organisms transform and use energy through metabolic processes.

Growth and development are also characteristics of living things. Growth involves an increase in size or number of cells, while development involves changes in an organism as it progresses through different stages of its life. These processes are controlled by genetic information and influenced by environmental conditions.

Reproduction allows organisms to produce new individuals. Reproduction can occur through different processes, including sexual and asexual reproduction. Although an individual organism may survive without reproducing, reproduction is important for the continuation of a species.

Living organisms can also respond to stimuli, which are changes in the internal or external environment. For example, plants may grow toward a source of light, while animals may move away from danger. These responses help organisms interact with and respond to conditions around them.

Homeostasis allows organisms to maintain relatively stable internal conditions even when their surroundings change. The body uses different processes to regulate factors such as temperature, water balance, and other internal conditions. This regulation helps organisms function properly.

Living organisms also interact with their environment. They depend on resources such as water, food, air, and suitable habitats. Over many generations, populations can undergo evolutionary change, allowing characteristics that help organisms survive and reproduce to become more common under particular environmental conditions.
example: A person sweating when their body becomes too warm is an example of a response involved in maintaining homeostasis. Sweating helps release heat from the body and contributes to maintaining a relatively stable internal temperature.
keyTakeaway: Living organisms perform essential life processes that allow them to survive, grow, reproduce, maintain internal stability, and interact with their environments. Understanding these characteristics helps distinguish living organisms from nonliving matter and explains how organisms function and respond to changes around them.
keyConcepts: Living organisms are made of one or more cells.
Cells are the basic structural and functional units of life.
Organisms obtain and use energy to perform life processes.
Metabolism refers to the chemical processes that occur within organisms.
Living organisms grow and develop.
Organisms reproduce to contribute to the continuation of their species.
Organisms respond to internal and external stimuli.
Homeostasis helps organisms maintain relatively stable internal conditions.
Living organisms interact with their environments.
Populations can change over generations through evolutionary processes.

title: Cell Structure and Functions
lesson:
The cell is the basic structural and functional unit of life. All living organisms are made up of one or more cells, and cells carry out the processes necessary for an organism to survive. Although cells differ in size, shape, and function, they share several basic structures.

Cells may be broadly classified as prokaryotic or eukaryotic. Prokaryotic cells do not have a membrane-bound nucleus, while eukaryotic cells have a membrane-bound nucleus and other specialized organelles enclosed by membranes.

Important cell structures include the cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, mitochondria, and ribosomes. Plant cells also have structures such as chloroplasts, a cell wall, and a large central vacuole. Each structure performs specific functions, and they work together to keep the cell functioning properly.
discussion:
The cell membrane forms the boundary of the cell and helps regulate the movement of substances into and out of the cell. It allows certain materials to enter while limiting the movement of others. This helps the cell maintain suitable internal conditions.

The cytoplasm is the region inside the cell membrane where many cellular processes take place. It contains the cell's organelles and provides an environment where various chemical reactions can occur.

In eukaryotic cells, the nucleus contains most of the cell's genetic material and helps control many of the cell's activities. The genetic information provides instructions that cells use for growth, development, and other life processes.

The mitochondria are organelles involved in cellular respiration, a process through which cells release usable energy from nutrients. Cells that require large amounts of energy often contain many mitochondria.

Ribosomes are structures involved in protein synthesis. Proteins are important because they perform many functions within cells and contribute to the structure and activities of organisms.

Plant cells contain chloroplasts, which contain chlorophyll and are the main sites of photosynthesis. Plant cells also have a cell wall, which provides additional support and helps maintain the cell's shape. The large central vacuole stores water and other substances and contributes to the structural support of plant cells.

Prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells differ in their internal organization. Prokaryotic cells, such as bacteria, do not have a membrane-bound nucleus or membrane-bound organelles. Eukaryotic cells, including plant and animal cells, have a nucleus and various specialized organelles.

Plant and animal cells share many structures, including a cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, mitochondria, and ribosomes. However, plant cells have additional structures such as a cell wall, chloroplasts, and a large central vacuole that are not found in typical animal cells.
example: Mitochondria are involved in cellular respiration, which provides usable energy for cellular activities. In plant cells, chloroplasts allow photosynthesis to occur, using light energy along with carbon dioxide and water to produce sugars that can be used by the plant.
keyTakeaway: Cells contain specialized structures that work together to carry out the processes needed for life. Understanding the functions of these structures helps explain how cells obtain energy, produce materials, maintain their internal conditions, and perform the activities necessary for living organisms.
keyConcepts: Cells are the basic structural and functional units of life.
Prokaryotic cells do not have a membrane-bound nucleus.
Eukaryotic cells have a membrane-bound nucleus and specialized organelles.
The cell membrane regulates the movement of substances into and out of the cell.
The nucleus contains genetic material and helps control cellular activities.
Mitochondria are involved in cellular respiration and energy release.
Ribosomes are involved in protein synthesis.
Chloroplasts allow plant cells to carry out photosynthesis.
The cell wall provides support and helps maintain the shape of plant cells.
The large central vacuole stores water and other substances in plant cells.
Plant and animal cells share several structures but also have important differences.

title: Biodiversity and Classification of Organisms
lesson:
Biodiversity refers to the variety of life on Earth. It includes the differences among living organisms, the variety of species, and the different ecosystems where organisms live. Biodiversity can be observed at three main levels: genetic diversity, which refers to differences within the same species; species diversity, which refers to the variety of species in an area; and ecosystem diversity, which refers to the variety of habitats and ecosystems.

Scientists use classification to organize and study the large number of organisms found on Earth. Classification groups organisms according to shared characteristics and, in modern biology, their evolutionary relationships. Taxonomy is the branch of biology concerned with naming, describing, and classifying organisms.

Organisms can be classified based on characteristics such as body structure, cell type, method of obtaining food, reproduction, and genetic similarities. Scientists use a hierarchical system of classification, which groups organisms into increasingly specific categories. Scientific names also help scientists identify organisms consistently, even when common names differ between places or languages.

Biodiversity is important because organisms are connected through food webs, nutrient cycles, pollination, decomposition, and other ecosystem processes. Plants, animals, fungi, and microorganisms all contribute to the functioning of ecosystems. Biodiversity also provides resources and benefits to humans, including food, medicine, materials, and ecosystem services.

However, biodiversity can be affected by habitat loss, pollution, overexploitation of natural resources, invasive species, and climate-related changes. Conservation involves protecting organisms, habitats, and ecosystems so that biodiversity can be maintained for future generations.
example:
A forest may contain many species of trees, flowering plants, insects, birds, mammals, fungi, and microorganisms. The variety of organisms represents species diversity, while differences among individuals of the same species represent genetic diversity. The forest itself is part of ecosystem diversity because it is one type of ecosystem among many others, such as wetlands, grasslands, coral reefs, and oceans.

Scientists can classify the organisms found in the forest by examining their characteristics and relationships. Conservation efforts, such as protecting forest habitats and preventing illegal wildlife collection, can help maintain this biodiversity.
keyTakeaway: Biodiversity represents the variety of life on Earth at different levels, from genetic differences within species to the variety of ecosystems. Classification and taxonomy help scientists organize and understand this diversity, while conservation helps protect organisms and ecosystems for the future.
keyConcepts: Biodiversity refers to the variety of life on Earth.
Biodiversity occurs at the levels of genetic diversity, species diversity, and ecosystem diversity.
Classification organizes organisms based on shared characteristics and evolutionary relationships.
Taxonomy involves describing, naming, and classifying organisms.
Scientific classification helps scientists identify and study organisms systematically.
Organisms interact with one another and contribute to ecosystem processes.
Conservation helps protect biodiversity, organisms, and their habitats.
discussion:
Biodiversity can be understood by looking at variety at several levels. Differences among individuals of the same species contribute to genetic diversity, the range of species in an area describes species diversity, and the variety of habitats represents ecosystem diversity. Considering these levels helps explain the different ways life is varied across Earth.

Classification helps scientists organize that variety. By comparing features such as body structure, cell type, reproduction, and genetic similarities, scientists can identify shared patterns and differences among organisms. A hierarchical system groups organisms from broader categories into more specific ones, while scientific names help people identify the same organism consistently when common names differ by place or language.

Biodiversity also supports food webs, nutrient cycling, pollination, and decomposition, and provides resources and other benefits to people. When habitats are lost or organisms are affected by pollution, overuse, invasive species, or climate-related changes, the variety and relationships within ecosystems can be affected. Protecting organisms and their habitats helps conserve biodiversity for the future.

title: Ecosystems and Environmental Sustainability
lesson:
An ecosystem is a community of living organisms interacting with one another and with the nonliving components of their environment. It includes both biotic factors, such as plants, animals, fungi, and microorganisms, and abiotic factors, such as sunlight, water, air, soil, temperature, and nutrients. These components are connected and influence how an ecosystem functions.

Energy moves through ecosystems mainly through feeding relationships. Producers, such as plants and algae, make their own food through processes such as photosynthesis and form the base of many food chains. Consumers obtain energy by feeding on plants or other organisms. Consumers may be herbivores, carnivores, omnivores, or organisms with other feeding strategies. Decomposers, including many fungi and bacteria, break down dead organisms and organic matter, returning nutrients to the environment.

Food chains show how energy is transferred from one organism to another, while food webs show the interconnected feeding relationships within an ecosystem. As energy moves through different trophic levels, some of it is used by organisms for life processes and released as heat. Nutrients, however, can be recycled through processes such as decomposition and nutrient cycling.

Ecosystems can be affected by changes in either biotic or abiotic factors. Human activities such as deforestation, pollution, overfishing, habitat destruction, and excessive resource use can alter ecosystems and reduce biodiversity. These changes may affect food webs, habitats, water quality, and the availability of natural resources.

Environmental sustainability focuses on meeting present needs while using natural resources responsibly so that they remain available for future generations. Sustainable practices may include protecting habitats, reducing waste, conserving water and energy, using resources efficiently, and supporting responsible management of ecosystems.

Understanding ecosystems helps people recognize that human communities are also connected to the natural environment. Protecting ecosystems is important not only for biodiversity but also for resources and environmental conditions that support human life.
example:
A mangrove ecosystem contains mangrove trees, fish, crabs, birds, microorganisms, water, soil, sunlight, and nutrients. Mangrove trees serve as producers, while animals such as fish and crabs act as consumers. Microorganisms and other decomposers help break down dead organic matter and return nutrients to the ecosystem.

Mangroves also provide habitats for many organisms and can help protect coastal areas from waves and erosion. Human activities such as cutting mangroves, pollution, and improper coastal development can affect the ecosystem. Protecting and restoring mangrove areas is an example of environmental sustainability because it helps conserve biodiversity and maintain important ecosystem functions.
keyTakeaway: Ecosystems depend on interactions among living organisms and nonliving environmental factors. Understanding how energy, organisms, and resources are connected helps people recognize the effects of human activities and the importance of protecting biodiversity and using natural resources responsibly for both present and future generations.
keyConcepts: Ecosystems contain interacting biotic and abiotic factors.
Producers make their own food and form the base of many food chains.
Consumers obtain energy by feeding on other organisms.
Decomposers break down dead organic matter and help recycle nutrients.
Food chains and food webs describe feeding relationships and energy transfer.
Human activities can change ecosystems and affect biodiversity.
Environmental sustainability promotes responsible use and management of natural resources.
Protecting ecosystems helps maintain biodiversity and important ecosystem functions.
discussion:
An ecosystem is a connected system in which living organisms and nonliving conditions affect one another. Plants, animals, fungi, and microorganisms are biotic components; sunlight, water, air, soil, temperature, and nutrients are abiotic components. A change in one part can influence the conditions and resources available to other parts of the ecosystem.

Feeding relationships show some of these connections. Producers provide the starting point for many food chains, consumers obtain energy by feeding on organisms, and decomposers break down dead matter and return nutrients to the environment. A food chain shows a pathway, while a food web shows how several feeding relationships are linked. These connections help ecosystems function, so major changes to organisms or their surroundings can affect ecosystem balance.

Activities such as deforestation, pollution, overfishing, habitat destruction, and excessive resource use can disrupt habitats and relationships among organisms. Environmental sustainability means using resources responsibly to meet present needs while keeping them available for future generations. Protecting habitats, conserving water and energy, reducing waste, and managing ecosystems responsibly are ways people can support this goal.
